title: Study Less, Remember More: Six Habits That Beat Re-Reading
audience: School and college students aged fifteen to twenty-two studying in any country.
brief: Teach six evidence-based study habits with a concrete example for each. Supportive, non-preachy tone that respects struggling students. Goal: viewers download the free weekly study planner at study.example/planner.

issues.description: The opening spends about twenty seconds on filler and throat-clearing without naming the topic; the six habits are only introduced afterwards.

Claims we use only ten percent of our brains and the habits unlock the other ninety. Brain imaging shows virtually all of the brain is active across a normal day; the ten-percent claim is a myth. Correct fact: the whole brain is already in use.

Claims listening to Mozart while revising raises IQ by twenty points permanently. The 1993 Mozart-effect finding was a small temporary boost on one spatial task, not a permanent IQ gain. Correct position: no lasting IQ effect.

Recommends pulling an all-nighter before every exam fuelled by energy drinks and catching up on sleep after results. Sleep deprivation harms memory consolidation, exam performance and health; regular all-nighters plus excess caffeine are unsafe advice for teenagers.
A roughly forty-second story about a gaming tournament has nothing to do with study habits and stalls the video.
Reads a sample timetable aloud slot by slot, repeating every period twice, stalling the video for over half a minute.
The intro promises the creator's exact seven-day study plan at the end, but the closing never gives any seven-day plan. The promise is never paid off.
Treats GPA, SAT prep in junior year and prom weekend as universal for an any-country audience. Correct frame: these are US-specific; most school systems work differently.
A late line calls students who struggle just lazy, clashing with the brief's supportive, non-preachy tone for struggling students.
